rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Three solubility ladders, one thermodynamic engine. Dissolution spends **lattice energy** and earns **hydration energy**; down Group IIA the growing M²⁺ loses hydration enthalpy fast (Be²⁺ −2494 → Ba²⁺ −1305 kJ/mol). With the **small OH⁻** anion, lattice energy collapses even faster, so the hydroxides **rise in solubility** — Be(OH)₂ insoluble and amphoteric, Mg(OH)₂ sparingly, Ca(OH)₂ lime water, Ba(OH)₂ a usable…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - ΔH(hydration): Be²⁺ ≈ −2494 → Ba²⁺ ≈ −1305 kJ/mol - Ksp(BaSO₄) ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰; solubility 2.4 mg/L - Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓ - Ca(OH)₂ ≈ 1.7 g/L; Ba(OH)₂ ≈ 56 g/L (20 °C) - Be(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂BeO₂ + 2H₂O (amphoteric)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Covers only: solubility of hydroxides, carbonates, sulphates of alkaline earth metals, general trend with explanation (within Chemistry of Metals).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The solubilities of the hydroxides of the alkaline earth metals increase, while those of their carbonates and sulphates decrease, with increasing atomic number of the metal."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Lime water vs baryta water*** — Ca(OH)₂ gives only ~1.7 g/L in water (hence the faint cloudiness of limewater with CO₂), while Ba(OH)₂ dissolves ~56 g/L — the same hydroxide chemistry, three rungs apart on the ladder, one test-tube apart in the lab.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Three Ladders, One Explanation The alkaline earth metals carry three solubility ladders that all point different ways: **hydroxides** get *more* soluble down the group, **carbonates** get *less* soluble, and **sulphates** collapse to near-insoluble barium sulphate. One thermodynamic argument — lattice energy vs hydration energy — explains all three, and NEB asks for it nearly every year.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The two competing energies - Dissolution pays two bills: breaking the crystal lattice (**lattice energy, ΔL**, always endothermic) and rewarding the ions with water (**hydration energy, ΔH, always exothermic**). Solubility follows the balance: hydration wins → soluble; lattice wins → insoluble.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Anion-size rule: OH- small -> solubility up; CO3^2-/SO4^2- big -> down. Endpoints: Ba(OH)2 soluble vs BaSO4 2.4 mg/L. Hydration numbers: Be2+ -2494, Ba2+ -1305. Be(OH)2 amphoteric.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): State and explain the general trends in the solubility of the hydroxides, carbonates and sulphates of the alkaline earth metals.** — **Hydroxides, M(OH)₂:** solubility **increases down the group** — Be(OH)₂ insoluble, Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble, Ca(OH)₂ sparingly (lime water), Sr(OH)₂ and Ba(OH)₂ appreciably soluble.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Why is MgSO₄ soluble in water but BaSO₄ practically insoluble?** — Dissolution must be paid for by the lattice energy and funded by hydration energy. **MgSO₄:** the small Mg²⁺ ion is very strongly hydrated (hydration enthalpy ≈ −1922 kJ/mol); this large exothermic hydration more than compensates the lattice energy, so…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The explanation must name both energies and say which falls faster for which anion — "hydration decreases" alone is half an answer.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: One competition, three ladders: hydration energy is the engine that falls at a fixed rate down the group, and the anion's size decides whether lattice energy falls faster (hydroxides rise) or slower (carbonates and sulphates sink).

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Dissolution = lattice energy (endothermic) vs hydration energy (exothermic); down IIA hydration of M2+ falls fast (Be2+ -2494 -> Ba2+ -1305 kJ/mol). Hydroxides (small OH-): lattice falls faster -> solubility increases: Be(OH)2 insoluble < Mg(OH)2 < Ca(OH)2 (lime water) < Ba(OH)2 soluble; basicity same order, Be(OH)2…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: BaSO₄'s Ksp of about 10⁻¹⁰ is so small that a single drop of BaCl₂ in a litre of sulphate solution precipitates essentially every sulphate ion — quantitative gravimetric analysis rests on this ladder's bottom rung.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Lattice energy** | Energy to separate 1 mol of ionic solid to gaseous ions | ΔL of BaSO₄ large | | **Hydration energy** | Energy released when gaseous ions are hydrated | Be²⁺ ≈ −2494 kJ/mol | | **Solubility product (Ksp)** | Equilibrium constant of dissolution | Ksp(BaSO₄) ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰ | |…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why the hydroxide ladder rises - OH⁻ is small (radius ~140 pm effective). In Be(OH)₂ the tiny Be²⁺ packs against the small OH⁻ → very high lattice energy. As M²⁺ grows, the lattice loosens rapidly (big cation, small anion = weak packing), while the cation's hydration loss is more gradual in relative terms — net: dissolution becomes easier.…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables **Ladder summary** | Group | Anion size | Lattice energy fall vs hydration fall | Solubility trend | |---|---|---|---| | M(OH)₂ | small | lattice falls faster | increases down | | MCO₃ | large | hydration falls faster | decreases down | | MSO₄ | large | hydration falls faster | decreases (sharply) down |

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: No verified PYQ on solubility trends exists in the bank; all items here are NEB-style practice.  ·  Explain with lattice and hydration energies why the hydroxide ladder rises while the sulphate ladder falls.  ·  Write the solubility order of the carbonates of Be, Mg, Ca, Ba and give one consequence of each end.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Use Ksp to explain why one drop of BaCl2 quantitatively precipitates sulphate.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **"Small anion → increasing solubility" is the rule, not "hydroxides are soluble":** Be(OH)₂ and Mg(OH)₂ are insoluble; only Ca(OH)₂ onward are usable in water — the ladder matters, not the label.  ·  **BaSO₄ insolubility is not "covalency":** it is the lattice/hydration balance; quoting "covalent character" misses the thermodynamic argument NEB wants.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Carbonates vs hydroxides directions are opposite:** memorise by anion size — small OH⁻ rises, big CO₃²⁻/SO₄²⁻ fall.  ·  ## 7. Exam Application **NEB-style (3m): State and explain the general trend in the solubility of the hydroxides, carbonates and sulphates of the alkaline earth metals.** — **Hydroxides:** solubility **increases** down the group — Be(OH)₂ is insoluble, Mg(OH)₂ sparingly, Ca(OH)₂ sparingly (lime water), Sr(OH)₂ more,…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Why is barium chloride solution used to test for sulphate ions, and why is MgSO₄ soluble while BaSO₄ is not?** — Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓ gives a dense white precipitate insoluble in acids — the definitive sulphate test.…
